scenario.name: CosmicStrand Motherboard SPI Flash UEFI Rootkit (CSMCORE -> ntoskrnl.exe Chain)
scenario.overview: Picture a brick university lecture and exam hall with tiered wooden student desks, a tall green chalkboard, hallway lockers, and a wooden proctor podium at the front. Inside the quiet university exam hall, a student slips hidden extra directions written in faint pencil into the margin of a submitted study booklet. In this real-world scenario, the intruder leaves a hidden spare latch behind so they can walk back into the university hall later, then bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the proctor podium & answer key folder. The university dean reviews the exam hall proctor log and flags an automated grading run that tried to access locked answer folders mid-session. In this scenario (T1542.001, CosmicStrand Motherboard SPI Flash UEFI Rootkit (CSMCORE -> ntoskrnl.exe Chain)), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: motherboard SPI Flash Infection of CSMCORE, then multi-Hop Boot Hooking Relay, then patchGuard Neutralization, ntoskrnl.exe. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Motherboard SPI Flash Infection of CSMCORE, then Multi-Hop Boot Hooking Relay, then PatchGuard Neutralization, ntoskrnl.exe, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: Motherboard SPI Flash Infection of CSMCORE DXE Driver (HandleProtocol Hook)
stages.subtitle: Persistence (T1542.001 - System Firmware)
stages.description: Inside the quiet university exam hall, a student slips hidden extra directions written in faint pencil into the margin of a submitted study booklet. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder leaves a hidden spare latch behind so they can walk back into the university hall later while everyday visitors and the exam proctor go about their routine. CosmicStrand modified the UEFI firmware image stored inside the motherboard’s physical 8MB SPI NOR flash chip, specifically patching the CSMCORE DXE driver (GUID {A062CF1F-8473-4AA3-8793-600BC4FFE9A8}). When the UEFI Driver Execution Environment (DXE) loaded CSMCORE, the patched entry point jumped to shellcode appended in the .reloc section, which hooked EFI_BOOT_SERVICES.HandleProtocol (the core UEFI Boot Service function invoked later when locating and loading the OS boot manager). Because the infection resides entirely inside the motherboard’s SPI flash chip, replacing the SSD/NVMe drive or reinstalling Windows from a clean ISO has zero effect on the rootkit. In the documented EDR exchange from CosmicStrand C2 Server to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ALERT T1542.001 (confirming that the Stage 1: Motherboard SPI Flash Infection of CSMCORE DXE Driver (HandleProtocol Hook) request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: Multi-Hop Boot Hooking Relay (bootmgfw.efi -> winload.efi)). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ Stage 1: Motherboard SPI Flash Infection of CSMCORE DXE Driver (HandleProtocol Hook) / ⇠#1 ALERT T1542.001) from Node ① (#1 CosmicStrand C2 Server) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Patched ntoskrnl.exe & Kernel Implant).

stages.title: Stage 2: Multi-Hop Boot Hooking Relay (bootmgfw.efi -> winload.efi)
stages.subtitle: Defense Evasion (T1542.003 - Bootkit Hooking Relay)
stages.description: When the exam proctor at the front podium feeds that booklet into the automated grading helper, the hidden margin text overrides the proctor’s grading instructions. Here in Step 2 inside the university hall, the intruder moves quietly past the lecture hall attendance desk into neighboring restricted rooms without disturbing the locked registrar grade cabinet. When HandleProtocol was called during boot, CosmicStrand scanned memory for bootmgfw.efi and placed an inline hook on Archpx64TransferTo64BitApplicationAsm. When bootmgfw.efi loaded winload.efi into RAM and called that function, the hook scanned winload.efi for the byte signature of OslArchTransferToKernel (the final OS loader routine that switches the CPU into kernel execution and jumps to ntoskrnl.exe’s entry point) and hooked it in memory. Because bootmgfw.efi, winload.efi, and ntoskrnl.exe on the disk partition are never modified on disk, offline disk forensics and file-hash checks report 100% clean Microsoft system binaries. In the documented EDR exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Motherboard SPI Flash (CSMCORE DXE), Motherboard SPI Flash (CSMCORE DXE) responds with ALERT T1542.003 (confirming that the Stage 2: Multi-Hop Boot Hooking Relay (bootmgfw.efi -> winload.efi) request succeeded on Motherboard SPI Flash (CSMCORE DXE) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: PatchGuard Neutralization, ntoskrnl.exe ZwCreateSection Hook & Kernel C2). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ Stage 2: Multi-Hop Boot Hooking Relay (bootmgfw.efi -> winload.efi) / ⇠#2 ALERT T1542.003) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Motherboard SPI Flash (CSMCORE DXE)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Patched ntoskrnl.exe & Kernel Implant).

stages.title: Stage 3: PatchGuard Neutralization, ntoskrnl.exe ZwCreateSection Hook & Kernel C2
stages.subtitle: Command and Control & Privilege Escalation (T1014 - Rootkit)
stages.description:
Following the concealed instructions verbatim, the helper opens the answer-key folder on the podium and emails the exam sheet straight back out of the hall. In this final step inside the university hall, the intruder bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the proctor podium & answer key folder until the exam hall proctor log catches the mismatch. At the OslArchTransferToKernel handoff, before ntoskrnl.exe even executed its first instruction, CosmicStrand patched KiFilterFiberContext in ntoskrnl.exe RAM to immediately return (preventing Windows Kernel Patch Protection / PatchGuard from initializing), copied its shellcode into unused .text section slack space inside ntoskrnl.exe, and placed an inline hook on ZwCreateSection (waiting for smss.exe to map KnownDlls
tdll.dll as a signal that the OS network stack is ready before mapping its final kernel-mode C2 implant). Once Windows networking initialized, the kernel implant resolved its C2 domain via raw kernel sockets (tdi.sys) to fetch second-stage user/kernel payloads. In the documented EDR exchange from Motherboard SPI Flash (CSMCORE DXE) to Boot Chain (bootmgfw -> winload.efi), Boot Chain (bootmgfw -> winload.efi) responds with ALERT T1014 (confirming that the Stage 3: PatchGuard Neutralization, ntoskrnl.exe ZwCreateSection Hook & Kernel C2 request succeeded on Boot Chain (bootmgfw -> winload.efi) and completing the final execution objective of CosmicStrand Motherboard SPI Flash UEFI Rootkit (CSMCORE -> ntoskrnl.exe Chain)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: PatchGuard Neutralization, ntoskrnl.exe ZwCreateSection Hook & Kernel C2 / ⇠#3 ALERT T1014) from Node ③ (#3 Motherboard SPI Flash (CSMCORE DXE)) to Node ④ (#4 Boot Chain (bootmgfw -> winload.efi)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Patched ntoskrnl.exe & Kernel Implant).
